notes.meaning: The psalm was likely written to celebrate a great rescue. Many think it was the night God destroyed the Assyrian army that was surrounding Jerusalem. God had made himself known to his people, Judah and Israel, by what he did for them. Where God is truly known, his name is honored as great.

Salem is the old name for Jerusalem, and Zion is the hill where God's house stood. God chose to live among his people there, and they came to worship him there. Salem means "peace," and the word for God's "tent" can also mean a lion's den. It pictures God as a lion guarding his home.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Augustine read God's dwelling "in peace" as a picture of the heart. You make room for God inside you by confessing your sins.

notes.meaning: Right there at Jerusalem, God broke every weapon the enemy brought, from flaming arrows to shields and swords. He won the whole war without his people lifting a hand. The victory came in answer to prayers made at God's house, such as King Hezekiah's prayer in the temple. "Selah" marks a pause to stop and think about this.

God shines with light and glory. The "mountains of prey" stand for proud, powerful empires like Assyria, which grew rich by robbing others. They are like mountains where wild beasts hunt. God is far greater than all of them. Their glory is to destroy, but his glory is to rescue.

The brave and boastful enemy soldiers were stripped of everything. They came to rob, and were robbed themselves. They "slept their last sleep," meaning they died. They could not even lift a hand, because God took away their courage and strength. Many link this to the night God's angel struck down the Assyrian army (2 Kings 19:35).

God did not need to strike a blow. One word of rebuke from him was enough. The war horses and the men who drove the chariots lay still, as if in a deep sleep. This echoes the Red Sea, where God threw horse and rider into the sea. "God of Jacob" reminds us that he is the God who keeps his promises to his people.

Not the Assyrian king, but God alone deserves our deepest awe and respect. When God is angry at sin, no one can stand against him. Spurgeon adds that people sheltered by Jesus' death in their place need not fear God's anger. That death is what Christians call the "atonement," which means being made right with God.

God spoke his judgment from heaven, and the whole earth went quiet in fear, like a courtroom when the judge stands up. He rose to rescue "the lowly": his humble, oppressed people who could not help themselves and cried to him. God's judgment on the wicked is the very thing that sets his people free. Though God may seem silent for a long time, sooner or later he acts for them.

Even people's rage against God ends up bringing him praise, because its failure shows how great his power is. Some read the second line as God holding back whatever anger would not serve his purpose, setting limits as he does for the sea. Others read it as God "wrapping himself" with wrath, like a soldier putting on a sword. Either way, even the worst evil stays under God's control.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the Hebrew text is unclear here and suggest a small correction. Then the verse would mean that those who escaped the enemy's anger hold a feast of thanks to God.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The old Greek and Latin Bibles read the verse differently. They say that human thought will praise God, and what remains of it will keep a feast day for him.

notes.meaning: After such a rescue, God's people should make promises to him and keep them. A vow binds you to God, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not keep it. The nations around should also honor God with gifts. God does not need anything from us. The gifts he wants most are our prayers, our praise, and our hearts.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Augustine taught that the psalm says "vow and pay," not "don't vow." Every believer should vow to believe, to hope for eternal life, and to live a godly life, and God's help makes it possible.

notes.meaning: The word for "breaks" pictures picking grapes from a vine. God can cut off the pride, courage, and even the life of rulers as easily as slipping a flower from its stem. Kings who frighten others are themselves afraid of him. Since no one can fight God and win, the wise thing is to submit to him.
